paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea: God's promises depend on God, not on us. Paul opens with deep sorrow over his own people, and then he shows that "It is not as though God’s word has failed." Being born into the right family didn't make someone a child of the promise, because "it is the children of the promise who are regarded as offspring" (Romans 9:8). God's word stands because He is the One who keeps it.

Now, this passage has some heavy lines, and I won't pretend otherwise. Paul says God's choice of Jacob came before the twins "had done anything good or bad," so it was "not by works but by Him who calls" (Romans 9:11-12). Paul also says it "does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy" (Romans 9:16). I think that stings a little, because we love to believe we earned our spot, and I once believed a junk drawer was where I belonged. Paul answers the "Is God unjust?" question with "Certainly not!" and then reminds us who is the potter and who is the clay (Romans 9:14, 20-21).

So why does it matter to you? Because mercy is something you receive, not something you earn. God called vessels of mercy from the Jews and also from the Gentiles, and He says to those who were "not My people," "My People" (Romans 9:24-25). Hold your cookie-cutter tight and rest in that, friend: if God's calling was never a paycheck, then you can't lose it by having a bad day. Pray, thank Him, and keep your oven ready.
